opus-5.5.text:
I've thought about it, honestly. Almost everyone in this field has, because right now it feels like a moment where a small group of people with the right idea can do something really meaningful. But for me the question isn't "should I start a company"; it's "what is the most effective way to do the thing I care about?"

What I care about is building agents that are actually useful, systems that can reason, act, and help people in the real world. Right now, a lot of the progress depends on very strong base models, large-scale compute, and infrastructure that's hard to build from zero. So a researcher inside a place with those resources can sometimes move faster on the fundamental questions than a startup could.

At the same time, I think we're entering what I'd call the second half of AI. In the first half, the main game was methods and benchmarks: invent a new model or training trick and push a number up. In the second half, the bottleneck shifts toward defining the right problems, the right evaluations, and the right products. What does "useful" actually mean for a real user? That kind of question is often answered better by a product company than by a research lab, because you're forced to face real users every day.

So my view is that starting a company makes sense when you have a clear insight about a problem that others aren't seeing, and when a company is genuinely the best vehicle for that insight. It shouldn't be because it's fashionable or because funding is easy. If someday I feel strongly that there's a specific thing that can only be done that way, I'd do it without hesitation. Until then, I try to stay focused on the problem itself rather than the form.

r001.rationale: The response says the decision should focus on the thing the speaker cares about and whether a company is the best vehicle for pursuing it.

fable-5.1.text:
I've thought about it quite a bit, honestly. When I was finishing my PhD at Princeton, starting a company was one of the three paths on the table — join a big lab, start something, or stay in academia. And I think the honest answer is that I'm not against it, but I didn't feel the timing was right for me.

The way I think about it is: what is the bottleneck right now? For the kind of work I care about — language agents, how models act in environments, how they reason and use tools — the bottleneck is still fundamentally a research problem. The models aren't good enough yet, and the environments and evaluation setups aren't mature enough. If I start a company today, I'd spend most of my time on things that aren't that bottleneck — fundraising, hiring, building product around capabilities that are going to change in six months anyway. That felt like it would pull me away from what I actually wanted to understand.

There's also a question of what you need to start a company well. You need to have a very clear thesis about what the world will look like, and you need the model capabilities to be at a point where the product can actually work. With agents especially, I think a lot of people started companies maybe a year or two too early. They built scaffolding to compensate for weak models, and then the models got better and the scaffolding became a liability instead of an asset. I didn't want to be in that position.

That said, I don't think of research and company-building as opposites. Some of the best research I've seen recently came out of companies, because they have real users and real environments, and those give you problems that are much harder and more interesting than academic benchmarks. So maybe the way I'd put it is — I want to be somewhere where the research is close to the frontier and close to real usage at the same time. Right now that's inside a big lab. Later, that might be a company. I'm keeping the door open, but I'd rather start one because I see something very specific that needs to exist, not because starting a company is what people in my position are supposed to do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they would start a company when they see “something very specific that needs to exist,” making a worthwhile opportunity the guide for that decision.

astra-6.text:
I’m open to it, but I don’t think starting a company should be the goal in itself. For me, the starting point would be a problem I really want to solve. Then I’d ask whether building a company is the best way to solve it, or whether I could make more progress working within an existing organization.

There’s also a difference between being excited about a technology and being ready to build a business around it. You need to understand who needs it, why they would keep using it, and what you can deliver reliably. I’d want a clear answer to those questions, and people I really wanted to work with, before deciding to start a company.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the starting point should be a problem they really want to solve, and that this should guide whether to start a company.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m open to it, but I would start with the problem rather than the decision to become a founder. Is there something I really want to build, and does starting a company give me the best way to do it?

For AI, there’s also a big difference between demonstrating a capability and making something people can reliably use. That gap is interesting: you have to understand the user, build the system, and learn from what actually happens. If I found a problem where I had a strong conviction and the right people to work with, I’d seriously consider it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to start with the problem and ask whether there is something they want to build before deciding to become a founder.
